chapters.title: Pick a topic you actually know
chapters.goal: Choose one specific topic people have genuinely asked you about more than once — the clearest signal of real demand.
explanation: Think back to questions people have asked you repeatedly — a skill, a hobby, a subject you help classmates with. Repetition is the signal that this knowledge is genuinely wanted.
Narrow the topic to a specific outcome, not a broad subject: not "guitar" but "learn your first 10 songs on guitar without reading sheet music."
Check that this specific angle isn't already covered extremely well and for free — if it is, find a more specific or differently-explained angle.
Outline the course in one sentence: what someone will be able to DO by the end, not just what they'll "learn about."
Test the idea before building anything — mention it to 5-10 people who'd be the target audience and see if they'd actually want it.
chapters.example: Liam kept getting asked by classmates how he edited his gaming clips so fast. He narrowed it to "edit a montage video in under 20 minutes using free software" — a specific, outcome-focused promise, not a vague "video editing basics" course.
mistakes: Picking a topic based on what seems popular rather than what people have genuinely asked you about.
Keeping the topic broad instead of narrowing to one specific, describable outcome.
Building the full course before testing whether anyone actually wants this specific angle.
chapters.template:
Course idea worksheet:
Repeated question/topic: ____
Specific outcome (what they'll be able to DO): "____"
Existing free coverage of this exact angle: ____
Tested with 5-10 people — reaction: ____
checklist: Identified a topic people have genuinely asked me about repeatedly
Narrowed to one specific, outcome-focused promise
Checked this specific angle isn't already covered well for free
Tested the idea with 5-10 real potential buyers before building

chapters.title: Know exactly who this is for
chapters.goal: Describe the specific person who's stuck right where your course starts, and know what would make them buy.
explanation: Your buyer is someone at a specific stuck point — not "anyone interested in the topic," but someone who's tried and hit a specific wall.
Figure out their current skill level precisely — a course pitched at the wrong level (too basic or too advanced) won't convert even genuinely interested people.
Research what free content already exists for this audience and identify the gap — usually depth, organization, or a faster path to the specific outcome.
Write a short profile: their current stuck point, what they've already tried, and what would make them trust your course to actually fix it.
Ask 2-3 people matching this profile directly what price and format (video, text, live) they'd actually want.
chapters.example: Liam's buyer profile: "Someone who's watched a dozen scattered YouTube tutorials but still can't put together a smooth montage in reasonable time." That precisely matched what his course promised to fix.
mistakes: Pitching to a vague, broad audience instead of someone at a specific stuck point.
Getting the skill level wrong, pitching too basic or too advanced for the real target buyer.
Never asking real target buyers what format or price they'd actually want.
chapters.template:
Audience one-pager:
Who: ____
Their specific stuck point: "____"
What they've already tried: ____
Format/price preference from real feedback: ____
checklist: Wrote the specific buyer profile and stuck point
Confirmed the right skill level for the target buyer
Researched the gap in existing free content
Asked real potential buyers about format and price preference

chapters.title: Price the product
chapters.goal: Set a price that reflects the value of the specific outcome, not just the length of content.
explanation: Price based on the value of the outcome (time saved, skill gained, problem solved) rather than by the hour of content — a focused 45-minute course solving a real problem can outprice a rambling 5-hour one.
Research 3-5 similar digital products/courses (even in adjacent topics) for a realistic price range.
Consider a launch price lower than your long-term price, explicitly framed as limited-time, to get early buyers and reviews faster.
Factor in the sales platform's fee (many take a percentage cut) when calculating real take-home per sale.
Decide whether to sell once at a fixed price or use a pay-what-you-want/tiered model — a simple fixed price is usually easiest to start with.
chapters.example: Liam priced his 45-minute focused course at $19, launched at $12 for the first week with that framed clearly as limited-time, and checked against similar creator-made mini-courses selling $15-30.
mistakes: Pricing based on content length instead of the value of the specific outcome delivered.
Not researching any comparable products before setting a price.
Forgetting the sales platform's fee when calculating real take-home per sale.
chapters.template:
Pricing plan:
Launch price: $____ (limited time)
Long-term price: $____
Comparable products researched: $____ – $____
Platform fee: ____% → real take-home per sale: $____
checklist: Priced based on outcome value, not content length
Researched comparable products for a realistic range
Considered a limited-time launch price
Calculated real take-home after platform fees

chapters.title: Tools and startup costs
chapters.goal: Confirm you can build and sell this for close to $0, and know what's actually worth spending on.
explanation: Free screen-recording tools and a sales platform with a free tier (taking a percentage per sale instead of an upfront fee) cover a real first product — this can genuinely start at $0.
The real cost here is TIME, not money — a focused course can take 15-30 hours to build well, which is worth planning for realistically.
If considering a paid tool (nicer screen recording, a course platform with more features), evaluate it against expected sales, not before any sales exist.
Avoid paying for "how to sell courses" meta-courses — the free documentation of your chosen sales platform, plus this app's own guidance, covers what's needed to start.
If a parent's card is needed for any paid tool, agree the amount together first.
chapters.example: Liam built his entire course with free screen-recording software and a free-tier sales platform that only took a percentage per sale — zero upfront cost, about 20 hours of his own time.
mistakes: Paying for expensive course-creation software before validating anyone wants to buy the course at all.
Underestimating the real time investment needed to build a genuinely good course.
Buying a "how to sell courses" meta-course instead of using free platform documentation.
chapters.template:
Startup cost sheet:
Tools used (free tier): ____
Estimated time to build: ____ hours
Any paid tool considered, and why: ____
checklist: Confirmed I can build and sell this with $0 upfront cost
Estimated the real time investment realistically
Avoided paid "how to sell courses" meta-products
Agreed any spending with a parent if their card is used

chapters.title: Present it professionally
chapters.goal: Make the product page and materials look trustworthy enough for a stranger to pay before seeing the actual content.
explanation: Write a product page that says exactly what the learner will be able to do by the end — the same specific outcome from chapter 1 — not a vague description.
Design a simple, clean cover image/thumbnail — free design tools make this a same-day task, and it's often the first thing a potential buyer judges.
Include a short preview (a free sample lesson or clip) so buyers can judge quality before paying — this builds crucial trust for a new, unproven creator.
Write 2-3 sample "who this is for" and "who this is NOT for" lines — being clear about who it's not for actually increases trust and conversion for the right buyers.
If you get early buyers' permission, add real testimonials to the page as soon as they exist.
chapters.example: Liam's product page opened with the exact outcome ("edit a montage in under 20 minutes"), included a 90-second free preview clip, and explicitly said "this isn't for people wanting professional cinematic editing — it's for fast, good-enough gaming content."
mistakes: A vague product description that doesn't state the specific outcome clearly.
No free preview, making it hard for a new, unproven creator to earn a stranger's trust before payment.
Trying to appeal to everyone instead of being clear about who it's specifically for.
chapters.template:
Product page checklist:
Specific outcome stated clearly? Yes/No
Cover image/thumbnail: done? Yes/No
Free preview included? Yes/No
"Who this is NOT for" line: "____"
checklist: Wrote a product page stating the specific outcome clearly
Made a simple, clean cover image
Included a free preview sample
Wrote a clear "who this is NOT for" line

chapters.title: Launch and get it in front of buyers
chapters.goal: Get the first wave of traffic to the product page from people likely to actually buy.
explanation: Announce it first to any existing audience you already have (social followers, a community you're part of) — warm traffic converts far better than cold.
If you don't have an existing audience, go directly to the specific community where your target buyer profile (from chapter 2) actually hangs out.
Create one or two pieces of content demonstrating a small, useful piece of the course's value for free — it proves the quality and naturally leads into the paid offer.
Time the launch around your limited-time launch price (from the pricing chapter) to create a genuine, honest reason to act now rather than later.
Track exactly where each sale came from so you know which channel to focus more effort on.
chapters.example: Liam posted a free "1 quick editing tip" video to his existing following, mentioned the full course was launching that week at a discount, and tracked that most sales came directly from that one video's link.
mistakes: Launching only to cold audiences instead of an existing warm one first, even a small one.
Not creating any free demonstration of value before asking people to pay.
Not tracking which channel actually drove sales, wasting effort on ones that don't work.
chapters.template:
Launch plan:
Warm audience I'll announce to first: ____
Free demonstration content: ____
Launch window (tied to limited-time price): ____
Sale source tracking: ____
checklist: Announced first to any existing warm audience
Created free content demonstrating real value
Launched within a clear, honest limited-time window
Tracked which channel each sale came from

chapters.title: Sell your first copies
chapters.goal: Get real strangers or your existing audience to buy and actually start the course.
explanation: Make sure the checkout and delivery flow actually works — buy it yourself (or have a friend) to confirm access arrives correctly before promoting widely.
Respond fast to any pre-purchase questions — for a new creator's first product, hesitation is normal and a quick, honest answer often closes the sale.
Welcome new buyers personally if the platform allows it (a short welcome message) — it's a small touch that builds trust for a new, unproven product.
Check in with early buyers partway through to see if they're actually progressing, not just to ask for a review immediately.
Log what led to each early sale — which piece of content, which specific question they asked — to understand what's actually convincing people.
chapters.example: Liam bought his own course through the checkout flow first to confirm delivery worked, then personally replied to every pre-purchase question in his community, closing several of his first ten sales that way.
mistakes: Promoting before confirming the checkout/delivery flow actually works.
Going silent on pre-purchase questions from a hesitant first-time buyer.
Asking for a review immediately at purchase instead of after they've had a chance to actually use it.
chapters.template:
First-sales log:
Checkout/delivery tested myself? Yes/No
Pre-purchase questions and my answers: "____"
Sale source | Buyer progress check-in done?
checklist: Tested checkout and delivery myself before promoting widely
Responded quickly to pre-purchase questions
Welcomed new buyers personally where possible
Checked in on buyer progress before asking for a review

chapters.title: Support buyers and collect feedback
chapters.goal: Help buyers actually finish and get the promised outcome, and use their feedback to improve the product.
explanation: Offer a simple way for buyers to ask questions while going through the course (email, a comment section, a community) — a support channel significantly increases completion and satisfaction.
Watch for where buyers commonly get stuck or drop off, if your platform shows any completion data, and treat that as the most valuable feedback for version 2.
Respond to every support question, even simple ones — for a small, early-stage product, this kind of personal attention is a real differentiator from bigger, more impersonal courses.
Ask for honest feedback (not just a star rating) from your first 10 buyers specifically, since detailed feedback is what actually improves the product.
Have a clear, fair refund policy stated upfront, and honor it without an argument if someone genuinely isn't satisfied.
chapters.example: Liam noticed from buyer questions that everyone got stuck on the same export-settings step. He added a short clarifying clip specifically for that step, which visibly reduced repeat questions afterward.
mistakes: No support channel at all, leaving confused buyers to give up silently instead of asking.
Ignoring a common sticking point instead of treating it as the most valuable feedback for improving the product.
No clear refund policy, or arguing with a genuinely dissatisfied buyer instead of honoring a fair policy.
chapters.template:
Support and improvement log:
Support channel: ____
Common sticking point noticed: "____"
Fix made in response: ____
Refund policy: "____"
checklist: Set up a simple support channel for buyers
Identified a common sticking point from buyer questions/data
Made a specific improvement based on that feedback
Stated a clear, fair refund policy

chapters.title: Getting paid
chapters.goal: Set up sales and payouts correctly and legally.
explanation: Most digital product sales platforms require an 18+ payout account holder — under that age, a parent opens and holds the account.
Understand the platform's payout schedule and minimum threshold before expecting a specific payout date.
Agree the transfer arrangement with the account-holding parent before the first sale.
Keep your own simple log of sales, separate from the platform dashboard, since platform access or reporting formats can change.
Never share account login details or one-time codes with anyone outside your agreed arrangement.
chapters.example: Liam's course sales went through his mother's account on the sales platform, with a written agreement that revenue transferred to Liam's own account monthly after the platform's payout cleared.
mistakes: Setting up a sales account without meeting the platform's age requirement.
Not understanding the payout schedule/threshold and being confused when money doesn't arrive as expected.
Sharing account access outside the agreed family arrangement.
chapters.template:
Payment setup record:
Platform account holder (18+): ____
Payout schedule and minimum threshold: ____
Agreed transfer arrangement to me: ____
checklist: Confirmed the account holder meets the platform's age requirement
Understood the payout schedule and threshold
Agreed the transfer arrangement with the account-holding parent
Kept my own separate sales log
chapters.parentNote: Digital product sales platforms generally require an 18+ payout account holder. A parent needs to hold this account under this age.

chapters.title: Accounting and taxes
chapters.goal: Track sales income and understand what's owed.
explanation: Digital product income is taxable business income in almost every country, including for minors, with specifics that vary by country.
Keep a log per sale: date, amount, platform fee, and net income — most platforms provide a sales export to help with this.
Set aside a portion of net income (a rough 20-25% placeholder is common) rather than spending it all immediately.
Watch for platforms that issue a tax form once you cross an earnings threshold, and keep your own records either way.
Have one real conversation with a parent, and once income is more than pocket change, check your country's actual rules for minors' business income.
chapters.example: Liam exported his sales data monthly and tracked net income (after the platform's fee) separately from gross revenue, setting aside a quarter of net income each month.
mistakes: Tracking gross sales instead of net income after platform fees.
Not exporting/keeping sales records independent of the platform's own dashboard.
Spending all sales income immediately with nothing set aside.
chapters.template:
Sales income log (one row per sale or per batch):
Date | Gross sales | Platform fee | Net income | Running total
Set-aside plan: ____% saved so far: $____
checklist: Started a running sales income log tracking net income
Set aside a percentage of net income
Checked whether the platform issues a tax form
Had one conversation with a parent about this income
chapters.parentNote: Digital product sales income is taxable in most places, including for minors. This needs a parent involved and a real check with local tax rules once income is meaningful.

chapters.title: Growing beyond the first launch
chapters.goal: Turn one successful launch into a repeatable, slowly-improving product line.
explanation: Use buyer feedback and completion data from the service chapter to release an improved version 2, rather than treating the first version as final.
Consider a second, related product for buyers who finished the first — an easier upsell than finding entirely new buyers.
Once you have real testimonials and a proven product, raise the price slightly from the launch price — social proof lets you charge more without losing conversion.
Keep promoting periodically rather than only at initial launch — most sales for a digital product happen well after the first-week spike, through ongoing mentions and content.
Review monthly: sales count, completion rate (if trackable), and buyer feedback themes — not just launch-week numbers.
chapters.example: After his initial launch, Liam used common buyer questions to release an improved version 2 with an extra module, raised the price once he had 15 genuine testimonials, and kept mentioning the course in his regular content instead of only at launch.
mistakes: Treating the first version as final instead of improving it with real buyer feedback.
Only promoting during the initial launch week and going silent afterward.
Never raising the price despite having strong, genuine social proof.
chapters.template:
Monthly growth review:
Sales this month: ____  Completion rate (if known): ____%
Feedback themes for version 2: ____
One promotion planned this month, beyond launch: ____
checklist: Used feedback/data to plan a version 2 improvement
Considered a second, related product for existing buyers
Raised price once real social proof existed
Kept promoting periodically beyond the initial launch
